warmup.q: Links between accounts and devices sit in an Oracle table account_identifier(account_id, identifier_id). You want the accounts that are exactly two steps from A-3101, where one step is "shares a device or phone". How many times does the query join account_identifier?
options: Once: the table already holds every link
Four times: each step goes from an account to its identifiers and back to other accounts
It can't be written in SQL
warmup.why: One step crosses the link table twice: from the account to its identifiers, then from each identifier to the other accounts that use it. Two steps is four joins of the same table, three steps is six, and "up to N" needs a recursive CTE. "One join per step" is the tempting answer because we say "one hop", but each hop through a shared identifier is two links. A graph store follows those links directly instead of joining.

sections.h: Every hop through a shared identifier is two more joins
sections.html:
The fraud team flags account A-3101 at 09:12 and asks one question: which other accounts are linked to it through a shared device or phone number, directly or through up to two more accounts in between? Store the links in a table first, the way you would in Oracle: account_identifier(account_id, identifier_id), with an index on each column.

One step, "accounts that share an identifier with A-3101", crosses the table twice. Find A-3101's rows through the index on account_id, then for each identifier find the other rows through the index on identifier_id. That's a self-join. Two steps is four joins, three steps is six, and "up to three" is a recursive CTE, lesson 6 of the SQL track, "Recursive CTEs: trees and graphs in SQL". The query grows with every hop you allow.

So does the work. Each lookup descends a B+tree, lesson 4 of the database internals track: about 3 or 4 pages for millions of rows, usually cached, so a few microseconds. And every step multiplies the rows: if each account has 3 identifiers and each identifier is shared by 2 accounts, every step fans out by about 6. One step touches 6 rows, three steps about 6 x 6 x 6 = 216, six steps about 47,000. The planner has to guess each intermediate size, and the guesses get worse with every join (lesson 10 of the database internals track, "Query optimization and cardinality estimates").

Now store the data the other way round. Put next to each account a list of the identifiers it uses, and next to each identifier the accounts that use it. A step becomes: read the list, jump to what it names, read that list. No search, so the cost of a hop doesn't depend on how many accounts exist. That is what a graph database stores. In Neo4j a node's record leads to its relationships, and each relationship records the nodes at both ends, so following one is a pointer read. Neo4j calls this index-free adjacency.

A graph store answers a question by walking: find a start node through an index, then follow relationships outward, and you pay for the part of the graph you touch. That's the picture for this lesson.

The fan-out doesn't go away. Both designs pay for every path they explore, and the Try-it shows a walk that jumps from 2 paths to 14 at the third step. What changes is the price of each hop and how easily you can say "up to N steps". If your questions are one or two hops of a known shape, stay in Postgres or Oracle. When they are paths of unknown length, rings or cycles, a graph store fits.

try.title: Start Neo4j and count what each step touches
steps: From the labs folder, start Neo4j 2026.10 Community: docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml up -d --wait (about 20 seconds on an idle laptop, longer on a busy one; up to 1.5 GB of Docker memory).

Load the fraud graph: docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml exec neo4j cypher-shell -f /sfz/nosql-11-fraud.cypher. It deletes whatever is there, then creates 13 accounts, 15 devices and phones, and the links between them.

Open a prompt with docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml exec neo4j cypher-shell and paste the two queries below. Before the second, predict how many paths and accounts each step adds. Leave Neo4j running for this lesson's other Try-its.

code.title: in cypher-shell
code.html: // one step out from the flagged account: account -USES-> identifier <-USES- account MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(other:Account) RETURN other.id AS account, x.id AS via; // one, two and three steps: how many paths, and how many accounts, at each MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3} (other:Account) WHERE other <> f RETURN size(x) AS steps, count(*) AS paths, count(DISTINCT other) AS accounts ORDER BY steps;

+---------------------+

+---------------------+

+--------------------------+

A-3101 shares two identifiers with A-3102, so step 1 is two paths to one account. Step 2 adds A-3103 through phone P-0199. Step 3 jumps to 14 paths and 6 new accounts: A-3104 and A-3105 through D-81 and P-0181, and four customers through a store kiosk that A-3103 also used. The work grew with the paths explored, not with the 13 accounts in the graph. cypher-shell also prints how long each query took; on a busy laptop the first queries take a few hundred milliseconds while Neo4j warms up.

sections.h: Nodes, relationships and properties, matched by drawing them
sections.html:
A property graph has two kinds of thing. A node is an entity: an account, a device, a phone number. It has one or more labels, which say what kind of thing it is (:Account, :Device), and properties, which are key-value pairs (id: 'A-3101', flagged: true). A relationship connects exactly two nodes. It has one type (USES, TRANSFERRED_TO), a direction, and properties of its own, such as amountMinor: 95000 on a transfer. If you think in tables, a node is a row and a relationship is a row of a join table, except that it's stored as a link, not computed by a join.

Cypher, Neo4j's query language, lets you draw the shape you're looking for in ASCII. Round brackets are nodes, arrows are relationships, square brackets hold the relationship's details:

MATCH (a:Account {id: 'A-1001'})-[:USES]->(x)
RETURN labels(x)[0] AS kind, x.id AS id

MATCH finds every place in the graph where the drawing fits, and binds the names (a, x) to what it found. WHERE filters the matches, RETURN says what to send back, and aggregates such as count(*) group by the other returned columns, with no GROUP BY. Direction matters: (a)<-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]-(sender) finds who paid a, and leaving the arrowhead off matches either way. CREATE writes a pattern, and MERGE matches it or creates it if it's missing, which is how you load events that may arrive twice.

Versions are worth a sentence, because they changed recently. Neo4j moved to calendar versions in 2025: this lesson runs Neo4j 2026.10.1, from October 2026. The query language is versioned separately. Cypher 5 is frozen and new features go into Cypher 25, which is the default in these releases; the PROFILE output later in this lesson says "Cypher 25". And there's now a standard: ISO/IEC 39075:2024, GQL, published in April 2024, the first new ISO database language since SQL in 1987. Its pattern matching grew out of Cypher, and Neo4j says Cypher already supports most of GQL's mandatory features. A MATCH ... RETURN like the one above reads the same in both.

try.title: Read, follow and write relationships
steps: In the same cypher-shell, paste the four queries below one at a time.
Before each, predict the rows. For the third: how many accounts sent money to A-1001, and what would change if you turned the arrow round?

code.title: in cypher-shell
code.html: // what does A-1001 log in with? labels(x) says what kind of node x is MATCH (a:Account {id: 'A-1001'})-[:USES]->(x) RETURN labels(x)[0] AS kind, x.id AS id ORDER BY id; // transfers of 900.00 or more: a property on the relationship MATCH (from:Account)-[t:TRANSFERRED_TO]->(to:Account) WHERE t.amountMinor >= 90000 RETURN from.id AS from, to.id AS to, t.amountMinor AS amountMinor ORDER BY amountMinor DESC; // direction matters: who sent money TO A-1001? MATCH (a:Account {id: 'A-1001'})<-[t:TRANSFERRED_TO]-(sender) RETURN sender.id AS sender, t.amountMinor AS amountMinor ORDER BY sender; // add a transfer, then read it back MATCH (a:Account {id: 'A-4001'}), (b:Account {id: 'A-2002'}) CREATE (a)-[t:TRANSFERRED_TO {amountMinor: 2500}]->(b) RETURN a.id AS from, type(t) AS rel, b.id AS to;

A-1001 logs in with one phone app, one phone number and the store kiosk: labels(x) tells the kinds apart, because the pattern (x) didn't name one. The 900.00-and-up transfers are the three that form the ring. Only two accounts paid A-1001: the arrow points into it. Turn the arrow round and you get the accounts A-1001 paid, which is A-2002 alone. The CREATE added one relationship with one property and returned it; reload the seed file if you want the graph exactly as it was.

sections.h: Quantified paths find the ring and the money cycles
sections.html:
The ring question repeats one step: account, identifier, account. Cypher 25 writes a repeated piece of a pattern as a quantified path pattern: the piece in brackets, followed by how many times it may repeat.

MATCH (start:Account {id: 'A-3101'})
      ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3}
      (other:Account)
WHERE other <> start
RETURN other.id AS account, min(size(x)) AS steps

{1,3} means one to three repetitions. The start node fills the first (:Account) of the first repetition, and other is the last account of the last one. A variable inside the brackets, x, becomes a list with one entry per repetition, so size(x) is the number of steps, and min(size(x)) is the shortest way to reach each account. The stepper walks this query one step at a time.

When the repeated piece is a single relationship, you can quantify the relationship alone. Money that comes back to where it started is a path of 3 to 6 transfers that ends at its first node:

MATCH p = (a:Account)-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6}(a)
RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.id] AS cycle

You'll also meet the older syntax, -[:TRANSFERRED_TO*3..6]->, in older code and blog posts. It still works, but Neo4j's manual says it isn't GQL conformant, and unlike a quantified path pattern it can't hold a WHERE inside the repeated part.

Two rules decide what comes back. Within one match, Cypher never uses the same relationship twice, so a path can't run back and forth over one link forever. And a cycle has no natural first node: the ring A-3101, A-3103, A-3104 is found once starting from each of its three accounts. The Try-it counts the copies; the lab keeps one by asking that the start has the smallest id in the cycle. The lower bound matters too. Two friends who pay each other back are a cycle of 2, which {3,6} leaves out on purpose.

try.title: Find the money cycles, then count the copies
steps: In the same cypher-shell, run the two queries below.
The seed has two cycles: three transfers between A-3101, A-3103 and A-3104, and four between A-3102, A-3105, A-4004 and A-3103. Predict how many rows the first query returns before you run it.

code.title: in cypher-shell
code.html: // money that comes back: 3 to 6 transfers that end where they started MATCH p = (a:Account)-[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6}(a) RETURN [n IN nodes(p) | n.id] AS cycle; // the older syntax for the same walk (not GQL conformant, still everywhere in the wild) MATCH p = (a:Account)-[:TRANSFERRED_TO*3..6]->(a) RETURN count(p) AS paths;

| ["A-3101", "A-3103", "A-3104", "A-3101"]           |

Seven rows for two cycles: the 3-cycle once from each of its 3 accounts, the 4-cycle once from each of its 4. The older *3..6 syntax finds the same 7 paths. A-4004 shares no device or phone with anyone, so the ring walk can't find it; the money finds it. A-1001 and A-2002 paying each other back is a cycle of 2, below the lower bound. The lab's money-cycles.cypher keeps each cycle once.

refs.title: Neo4j Cypher Manual: variable-length patterns (quantified path patterns and relationships)

sections.h: Start from an index, and keep supernodes out of the walk
sections.html:
Every walk starts somewhere, and the start is the one place a graph needs an index. Without one, MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) reads every Account node and filters them: NodeByLabelScan, then Filter. On 13 accounts that's 14 database hits. On 10 million it's 10 million, before the first hop. A uniqueness constraint on Account.id also builds an index, and the plan starts with NodeUniqueIndexSeek instead: 2 hits, whatever the size. The Expand(All) operators after it are the walk, and they don't change. PROFILE runs a query and shows this plan with the rows and hits of every operator, like EXPLAIN ANALYZE in Postgres.

The second thing to watch is the node everyone touches. The store kiosk in the lab's graph has 5 accounts. A real kiosk, a shared office Wi-Fi address or a payment processor's test card can link 50,000 accounts, and every walk that passes through it brings all of them in. That's a supernode. You have three ways out. Filter it out inside the pattern by a property, as ring.cypher does with the kiosk. Cap the degree, with WHERE COUNT { (x)<-[:USES]-() } < 50 on the identifier. Or don't model it: an identifier that thousands of people share proves nothing about fraud, so don't create the relationship at all.

Know when a graph is the wrong store. "Total payments per merchant per day" visits every transfer and follows nothing, which is a job for a columnar store or a Postgres aggregate. A ledger that takes thousands of writes a second wants the payments store, not a graph. In practice the graph is a second copy, fed from the system of record: the payments service writes Oracle, a Kafka topic carries the events, and a consumer MERGEs accounts, devices and transfers into Neo4j for the fraud team's walks. The worked example builds that consumer.

try.title: Find the supernode, then watch the start of the plan change
steps: In the same cypher-shell, run the block below. The first query ranks identifiers by how many accounts use them.
Compare the two PROFILE plans: which operator changed, and how many database hits did it save?
Stop Neo4j when you're done: docker compose -f env/neo4j.yml down -v.

code.title: in cypher-shell
code.html: // which identifiers do the most accounts share? MATCH (x)<-[:USES]-(a:Account) RETURN labels(x)[0] AS kind, x.id AS id, count(a) AS accounts ORDER BY accounts DESC, id LIMIT 3; PROFILE MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(other:Account) RETURN other.id AS account, x.id AS via; CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE; PROFILE MATCH (f:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(other:Account) RETURN other.id AS account, x.id AS via;

refs.title: Neo4j Cypher Manual: MERGE (and why it needs a uniqueness constraint under concurrency)

analogy: A graph database is a city map and a walk. Tables are a phone book: to go from one person to the people they share an address with, you look the person up, read the address, then search the whole book by address, once per step. On a map you put your finger on the house and follow the streets: each step goes from where you are to the next corner, however big the city is. The index is the street directory you use once, to find the first house. A supernode is the central station: every walking route through it suddenly reaches half the city. The analogy breaks on one point: a real map shows every street at once, but the database only ever sees the streets your walk follows, so a badly bounded walk can wander into far more of the city than you meant.
world: Your fraud checks today are probably rules in the authorization path plus a nightly SQL job that joins accounts, devices and cards. The nightly job is where the graph pays off: "accounts within three shared identifiers of a confirmed fraudster" or "money that came back to its sender within an hour" are walks, and in SQL they are recursive CTEs that the optimizer struggles to estimate. Keep Oracle as the system of record. Feed Neo4j from the Kafka topics you already have (logins, device fingerprints, transfers) with a consumer that MERGEs each event, so redeliveries don't duplicate anything. The authorization path should call a precomputed risk flag, not run a graph walk inside a 120 ms budget.
mistake: The most common mistake is an unbounded walk from an unindexed start: MATCH (a:Account {id: $id})-[:USES*]-(b:Account) with no constraint on Account.id and no upper bound. It works on the test graph, so people ship it. In production the start is a label scan over millions of accounts, and the walk passes through one kiosk or shared Wi-Fi address and reaches most of the graph, so the query runs for minutes and fills the heap. The fix has three parts: a uniqueness constraint on the property you start from, an upper bound on every quantifier ({1,3}, not *), and a filter or a degree cap for identifiers that thousands of accounts share.

compare.title: The ring around A-3101, up to three steps, in SQL and in Cypher

a.label: PostgreSQL: recursive CTE
a.title: a link table account_identifier(account_id, identifier_id)
a.html: WITH RECURSIVE ring(account_id, steps, path) AS ( SELECT 'A-3101'::text, 0, ARRAY['A-3101'] UNION ALL SELECT b.account_id, r.steps + 1, r.path || b.account_id FROM ring r JOIN account_identifier a ON a.account_id = r.account_id -- my identifiers JOIN account_identifier b ON b.identifier_id = a.identifier_id -- their other users AND b.account_id <> ALL (r.path) -- never walk back WHERE r.steps < 3 ) SELECT account_id, min(steps) AS steps FROM ring WHERE steps > 0 GROUP BY account_id ORDER BY steps, account_id;

b.label: Neo4j: quantified path pattern
b.title: Cypher 25
b.html: MATCH (start:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3} (other:Account) WHERE other <> start RETURN other.id AS account, min(size(x)) AS steps ORDER BY steps, account;

compare.note: Both return the same eight accounts on the lab's graph (I ran the SQL on PostgreSQL 18 to check). The SQL spells out the walk: a seed row, a recursive step that joins the link table twice, a path array so it doesn't walk back, and a depth counter. Every step is two index lookups and a join, and the planner has to estimate the size of a recursion it can't see the end of. The Cypher draws one step and says how often it repeats; Neo4j follows stored relationships and never uses the same relationship twice in a path. Neither stops a supernode from flooding the result: both need the kiosk filtered out explicitly.

worked.title: Feed the fraud graph from Kafka without duplicates

steps.say: Start from the event. The login service publishes one record per login to a Kafka topic, keyed by account. Kafka delivers each record at least once, so the consumer will sometimes see the same login twice.

First try: CREATE the account, the device and the link. A redelivered record creates a second A-3101 node and a second relationship. Every walk then counts the duplicate, and the ring query reports A-3101 as its own neighbour.
steps.code: // wrong: every delivery adds new nodes and a new relationship CREATE (a:Account {id: $accountId})-[:USES]->(d:Device {id: $deviceId})

steps.say: Use MERGE, piece by piece. Each MERGE matches the pattern if it exists and creates it if not. Merging the nodes separately, then the relationship between them, means an existing account is reused instead of a whole new path being created. ON CREATE SET runs only the first time.
steps.code: MERGE (a:Account {id: $accountId}) MERGE (d:Device {id: $deviceId}) MERGE (a)-[u:USES]->(d) ON CREATE SET u.firstSeen = datetime($at) SET u.lastSeen = datetime($at)

steps.say: Add the constraints. Neo4j's manual is plain that under concurrent writes MERGE alone guarantees the pattern exists, not that it is unique; two consumers handling two partitions can both create A-3101. A uniqueness constraint closes that race and gives every MERGE an index seek instead of a label scan.
steps.code: CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE; CREATE CONSTRAINT device_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (d:Device) REQUIRE d.id IS UNIQUE;

steps.say: Run it from the Kafka consumer with the Neo4j Java driver 6.3. executableQuery runs the statement in a transaction and retries it on transient errors, and the parameters keep the statement text constant, so Neo4j plans it once.
steps.code: // a $$ string (Kotlin 2.2 and later): a single $ stays a literal $, which Cypher needs for parameters val merge = $$""" MERGE (a:Account {id: $accountId}) MERGE (d:Device {id: $deviceId}) MERGE (a)-[u:USES]->(d) ON CREATE SET u.firstSeen = datetime($at) SET u.lastSeen = datetime($at) """.trimIndent() for (record in consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500))) { val login = parse(record.value()) // accountId, deviceId, at driver.executableQuery(merge) .withParameters(mapOf("accountId" to login.accountId, "deviceId" to login.deviceId, "at" to login.at)) .execute() } consumer.commitSync() // after the writes: a crash means a replay, and MERGE absorbs it

lab.title: Write the fraud team's four queries in Cypher, against a real Neo4j
steps: Make sure Docker is running, then run the tests from the labs folder. The first run starts one neo4j:2026.10.1 container through Testcontainers, which takes up to a minute or two. Before every test the graph from the lesson is reloaded. One test passes (it only checks the seed); eight fail.

Each exercise is one .cypher file holding a placeholder query. The comment at the top gives the parameters, the columns and the order the tests expect. You can try a query in the lesson's cypher-shell first.
Write schema.cypher: one statement that creates a uniqueness constraint named account_id on Account.id. One test passes.

Write suspicious-pairs.cypher and ring.cypher. The ring test runs your query with and without the kiosk, and a plan test checks that it starts with NodeUniqueIndexSeek once the constraint exists. Five more pass.
Write money-cycles.cypher, with each cycle once. All nine pass.
hints: A uniqueness constraint: CREATE CONSTRAINT account_id IF NOT EXISTS FOR (a:Account) REQUIRE a.id IS UNIQUE.

Pairs: match (a:Account)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(b:Account) WHERE a.id < b.id, then WITH a, b, x ORDER BY x.id before collect(x.id), so the list comes out sorted. Filter with WHERE size(shared) >= $minShared after the WITH.
Ring: inline a filter on the identifier in the repeated part: (x WHERE NOT coalesce(x.kind, '') IN $skipKinds). Phones have no kind, which is why coalesce is there.

Cycles: -[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6} back to the same (a), and WHERE all(n IN nodes(p) WHERE a.id <= n.id) keeps the rotation that starts at the smallest id. reduce(total = 0, t IN relationships(p) | total + t.amountMinor) adds up the amounts.
A trailing ; is fine; the tests strip it. Comments start with //.

drill.title: The ring query from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lesson and the lab. Write the Cypher that returns every account one to three steps from A-3101 (one step = account, shared device or phone, account), skipping identifiers whose kind is 'store kiosk', with the fewest steps to each. Then write one sentence on what makes the query start fast.

answer.html: MATCH (start:Account {id: 'A-3101'}) ((:Account)-[:USES]->(x WHERE coalesce(x.kind, '') <> 'store kiosk')<-[:USES]-(:Account)){1,3} (other:Account) WHERE other <> start RETURN other.id AS account, min(size(x)) AS steps // x holds one identifier per step ORDER BY steps, account; // Fast start: a uniqueness constraint on Account.id gives the planner an index, // so the walk begins with NodeUniqueIndexSeek instead of scanning every Account.

recap: In tables, one step through a shared identifier is two lookups in a link table and a join; "up to N steps" is a recursive CTE that grows with every hop. A graph store keeps each node's relationships with it, so a hop is a pointer read.
A property graph has nodes (labels and properties) and relationships (one type, a direction, properties). Cypher matches a pattern drawn in ASCII: (a:Account)-[:USES]->(x).

Quantified path patterns repeat a piece of a pattern, ((...)-[:USES]->(x)<-[:USES]-(...)){1,3}; -[:TRANSFERRED_TO]->{3,6} quantifies one relationship. The older *3..6 still works but isn't GQL conformant.
A walk starts from an index (a uniqueness constraint gives you one: NodeUniqueIndexSeek instead of NodeByLabelScan) and pays for the paths it explores. Bound every walk and keep supernodes out of it.

Neo4j uses calendar versions (2026.10) and Cypher 25 by default; GQL, ISO/IEC 39075:2024, standardised the pattern style Cypher started. Use a graph for walks, rings and cycles, fed from the system of record, not as the ledger.

explain.prompt: A colleague says: "We have indexes on everything in Oracle; a graph database can't be faster at following links than an indexed join." Explain what each one does per hop, where the graph store really wins, and where it doesn't.
explain.answer: Per hop, Oracle finds the next rows through an index: it descends a B-tree, a few page reads that are usually cached, then joins. A step through a shared device is two of those, one to find the account's devices and one to find the devices' other accounts, and "up to three steps" becomes a recursive query that the optimizer has to estimate blind. A graph store keeps each node's relationships with the node, so a hop is a pointer read whose cost doesn't depend on how many accounts exist, and the query is a pattern with a repeat count instead of a recursion. Both still pay for every path they explore: one shared kiosk can turn 3 accounts into 4,800 in either system, so you bound the walk and filter supernodes either way. The graph wins for walks of unknown length, rings and cycles, which is exactly the fraud team's work. It loses for whole-table aggregations and for being the ledger: those stay in Oracle, and we feed the graph from Kafka with MERGE and uniqueness constraints so replays don't duplicate anything.

deeper.html:
Cypher's default match mode is "different relationships": within one match, no relationship appears twice, but a node may. That's why a ring walk can come back through the start account by a different identifier, and why WHERE other <> start is needed. Cypher 25 lets you name the mode: MATCH DIFFERENT RELATIONSHIPS is the default (GQL calls it DIFFERENT EDGES), and MATCH REPEATABLE ELEMENTS lets a path reuse relationships. On the lab's graph, (a:Account {id: 'A-3101'})-[:USES]-{2}(b) finds 2 paths by default and 4 with repeatable elements: the extra two go out to a device and straight back. A walk that may repeat must be bounded, or it never ends.

For "how far apart are these two accounts", ask for the shortest path instead of listing every path: MATCH p = SHORTEST 1 (a:Account {id: 'A-3101'})(()-[:USES]-()){1,8}(b:Account {id: 'A-4003'}) RETURN length(p). On the lab's graph it returns 6 relationships, from A-3101 through D-77, A-3102, P-0199, A-3103 and the kiosk to A-4003. It stops at the shortest match rather than enumerating every route, which matters as soon as a supernode is in reach.

Neo4j Community runs one standalone server. Clustering (primary servers that agree through Raft, plus secondaries that serve reads) is in the Enterprise edition, and so is online backup. For a fraud graph that is rebuilt from Kafka, a standalone server plus a replayable topic is a defensible design: losing the server costs a rebuild, not data.

Graph algorithms are a separate tool from pattern matching. Neo4j's Graph Data Science library computes things like PageRank, community detection (which accounts form tight clusters) and node similarity over the whole graph, in memory. Fraud teams often run community detection nightly, store each account's community id as a property, and then match patterns within a community. The patterns in this lesson tell you how two accounts are connected; the algorithms tell you which groups exist at all.

SQL is getting graph queries too. SQL/PGQ, part 16 of the SQL:2023 standard, adds GRAPH_TABLE with a MATCH clause whose syntax is close to Cypher and GQL. Oracle Database 23ai supports SQL/PGQ property graph queries over ordinary tables, which may be the shortest path from your existing schema to your first graph query.
